speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS conducts monetary policy by managing the nominal effective exchange rate of the Singapore dollar, the S$NEER, within a policy band.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When global financial or economic conditions cause the S$NEER to be subject to significant strengthening or weakening pressures that are inconsistent with domestic price stability, MAS may intervene in the foreign exchange market to sell or buy Singapore dollars, to keep the S$NEER within the policy band.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Official Foreign Reserves (OFR) plays an important role in the MAS’ conduct of monetary policy and support of financial stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It gives confidence in Singapore's exchange rate-centred monetary policy framework, particularly during periods of speculative pressure or financial crises, when MAS will need to use its OFR to purchase Singapore dollar to defend the exchange rate.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Conversely, in periods of appreciation pressures on the Singapore dollar, MAS can also sell Singapore dollar in exchange for foreign currency to keep the S$NEER within the policy band.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When this happens, MAS accumulates foreign assets and its OFR grows.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS invests the OFR mainly in safe and liquid assets, so as to ensure that the OFR is available at short notice when needed – for example, to fend off a speculative attack on the Singapore dollar which could potentially undermine confidence in the Singapore economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore's excess of domestic savings over investments and persistent capital inflows – in part, reflecting Singapore's triple-A credit rating and the abundant liquidity in global financial markets – have meant strong appreciating pressures on the Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If left unchecked, the S$NEER will strengthen much more than necessary to keep inflation low and stable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As MAS intervened in the foreign exchange market to dampen appreciation pressures on the S$NEER, it has been steadily accumulating OFR beyond that which it estimates is required to fulfil its monetary policy and financial stability mandate.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is no strict formula to determine this range, but it takes reference from a range of internationally used measures of reserve adequacy that recognise the foreign currency needs of our small open economy that is heavily dependent on trade and financial transactions with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS has assessed that this amount of OFR should be able to provide a sufficient buffer against severe crises in the global economy and financial markets.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is significantly above the range which I just mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It would be inefficient for MAS to hold on to OFR beyond its needs, because returns on the OFR will be limited by MAS' relatively safer and more liquid investment posture as a central bank.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, it is for this reason that GIC was set up in 1981 to invest OFR that was not needed by MAS in longer-term, high-yielding assets rather than in liquid but low-yielding assets.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The transfer of OFR from MAS to the Government for management by GIC has therefore been a long-standing practice.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, in 2019, MAS announced a transfer to the Government of S$45 billion of OFR after reviewing the optimal amount of OFR needed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To date, transfers of MAS' OFR to the Government have been facilitated through a corresponding reduction in the Government's Singapore dollar cash deposits with MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, there is a reduction of assets on MAS' balance sheet, which is matched by a reduction of liabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: However, this transfer mechanism is increasingly facing constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is mainly because MAS' accumulation of OFR has in recent years persistently outpaced the growth of Government's deposits with MAS, which are not growing as quickly due to smaller fiscal balances.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is far in excess of the Government’s current deposits with MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we need a new instrument to effect the transfer of assets from MAS to the Government for long-term investment management.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To be clear, this transfer of assets does not increase the total size of the Government’s reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is about shifting assets from MAS to the Government as part of long-term investment management by the GIC.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments will allow MAS to subscribe for RMGS issued by the Government under the Government Securities Act (GSA), as consideration for OFR that is transferred to the Government for longer-term investment management by GIC.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In introducing this Bill, MAS and the Government have sought to ensure that MAS' ability to fulfil its mandate is not affected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Two sets of safeguards have therefore been proposed in both the MAS Act and the GSA to tightly circumscribe the conditions for MAS’ subscription of RMGS and the Government’s issuance of RMGS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will provide further details about each set of safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The first set of safeguards seeks to robustly address potential misperceptions of monetary financing, in other words, MAS financing the Government's spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, MAS is already prohibited under the MAS Act from lending to the Government or subscribing for Government securities, apart from limited exceptions, such as to conduct monetary policy or to develop the bond market in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Similarly, there are existing safeguards under the GSA today, where the Government’s proceeds from borrowing are accounted for in the Government Securities Fund and can only be used for investments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Thus, borrowings by the Government in the form of RMGS, will not increase the amount available for spending by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will add safeguards in the MAS Act and the GSA to avoid any misperception that RMGS will constitute monetary financing of Government spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, the Bill will empower MAS to subscribe for RMGS for the sole purpose of facilitating the transfer of OFR to the Government and MAS can do so only if the subscription does not compromise its objective of ensuring medium-term price stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, the Bill will require MAS to use only foreign assets to subscribe for RMGS; and correspondingly, the Government to accept only foreign assets in exchange, to be accounted for in the Government Securities Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This draws a clear and direct link between MAS’ RMGS subscription and the transfer of MAS’ OFR to the Government and eliminates the possibility that MAS as a central bank creates Singapore dollars to finance Government spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The bulk of the remainder is estimated based on the expected pace of OFR accumulation in future years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The separate net issuance limit differentiates RMGS from other types of Government borrowings.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Transfer amounts and hence RMGS issuance depends on the accumulation of OFR which is driven mainly by MAS' conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This, in turn, is affected by financial market factors that can be uncertain.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Having a separate limit for RMGS will ensure that the planned issuances of other Government securities and Treasury Bills are not affected should the issuance of RMGS be higher than projected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Conversely, it will also avoid creating additional unintended borrowing space for other Government securities and Treasury Bills, should RMGS issuance be lower than expected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government Financial Statements will also state the total gross issuance and total gross redemption of RMGS, in addition to the outstanding RMGS amount.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, that is the first set of safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A second set of safeguards will preserve MAS' access to sufficient OFR to fulfil its mandate of conducting monetary policy and ensuring financial stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill sets out in the MAS Act that any subscription for RMGS can only be made for the purposes of transfer of OFR in excess of the amount MAS considers necessary for the conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS alone determines the amount of OFR required to meet its mandate and consequently, the amount of OFR which can be transferred to the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government plays no role in this decision.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Consequently, MAS also determines the amount and timing of its RMGS subscriptions to effect transfers of OFR, and the Government cannot independently effect a transfer of OFR from MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill also sets out in the GSA that RMGS will be issued subject to such conditions as to repayment and redemption as may be agreed between MAS and the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These conditions will safeguard MAS' access to sufficient OFR to implement monetary policy and support financial stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, MAS will have the right to redeem RMGS before maturity at par, to meet its OFR needs in support of the conduct of monetary policy and financial stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We expect that the optimal amount of OFR held by MAS will comfortably meet its needs under most circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Hence, MAS' redemption of RMGS before maturity will likely be needed to supplement OFR only in a tail risk event.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When MAS redeems RMGS at or before maturity, MAS will be repaid in foreign assets.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These conditions will ensure that the RMGS on MAS' balance sheet can readily support MAS' ability to fulfil its mandate if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: RMGS will enable such transfers to be sustained over the longer term.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While the Government will take on more debt as a result of RMGS, borrowing is not revenue and the introduction of RMGS does not increase what the Government can spend.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This Bill will also put in place safeguards to ensure that RMGS will not and cannot be used for Government spending, and that MAS will continue to have ready access to the transferred OFR to support MAS’ ability to fulfil its mandate as necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Further, the nominal increase in Government debt through RMGS will be matched by an increase in assets, with no change in the Government’s net asset position.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government continues to have a strong balance sheet with no net debt.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: RMGS does not change this, as all RMGS issuances are only used to facilitate transfers of assets for longer-term investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the financial investments front, the Singapore dollar denominated equity and debt market assets continue to attract significant capital inflows as investors take comfort in our solid sovereign ratings, our strong economic fundamentals and political stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Coupled with the country's net positive savings, our local dollar persistently faced strong appreciation pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In order to manage the Singapore dollar within a tolerated trade-weighted band, MAS would often need to intervene in the foreign exchange markets to moderate the rise of the Singapore dollar and as a result, accumulate a growing size of foreign currency, known as the Official Financial Reserves (OFR).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To many jurisdictions, this would be an enviable position or a happy problem to manage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It demonstrates the international markets' confidence in the Singapore’s economy, the securities that we issued and the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While this may be a happy situation, we need to manage a couple of related issues.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In excess of that OFR, what do we do with the accumulated OFR which are in foreign currencies?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How can we derive decent returns from these accumulated funds?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The current level of OFR represents more than 100% of the size of Singapore's GDP.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Minister mentioned that it is about 110% or 111% of the GDP.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I suppose this takes into consideration the size and the daily turnover of the Singapore dollar traded in markets and the ability to buffer against large and sudden outflows of capital that could result in extreme volatility in the Singapore dollar exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To serve this function of managing extreme volatility, the OFR are kept in cash or high-quality liquid assets so that it can be drawn upon immediately when the need arises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whether in absolute amount or relative to the GDP or on a per capital basis, our OFR stock would be among the highest in the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, there are no real merits to further add to the stock of the OFR if the optimal level is already more than adequate to manage monetary operations and to tackle markets' tail risk events.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides, we also have two other pots of national reserves managed by GIC and Temasek, which could further shore up confidence and strength in Singapore's financial position.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While the OFR amount is regularly published, I would like to take this opportunity in this Second Reading to ask the Minister to share on the framework under which the OFR are managed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What are the liquidity and risk guidelines and is there a target return for MAS in managing the OFR?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, how often does MAS review the optimal level of OFR to hold and do significant economic or market risk events such as a regional currency crisis immediately trigger upward adjustments of the OFR?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With this transfer, the excess OFR can be invested in portfolios with longer-term horizons and relatively more risky assets so as to achieve higher returns than what MAS can deliver.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This instituted transfer mechanism sharpened the clarity of the role between MAS, which primarily focuses on price stability; and GIC, which invests for longer tenures and take on higher risks for higher returns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, on this aspect, I have two further questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Would the excess OFR that is being transferred to GIC be managed as a segregated pot from the rest of the financial reserves that GIC manage?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is, would the returns from these excess reserves contribute to the annual NIRC?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As to whether the Government could use the RMGS proceeds to finance Government spending, I am satisfied that the current legislative safeguards, namely the GSA and the current amendments to the MAS Act, are adequate to prohibit that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, the Constitution also requires the Government of the day to balance the budget over its term of Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The present Bill introduces important institutional safeguards consistent with this Government's overall approach of designating different accounts for distinct financial functions that are designed to inhibit the purchase of Reverse Management Government Securities, or RMGS, for the purposes of either monetising Government expenditures or financing fiscal deficits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also embeds several related amendments to the Government Securities Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As with the earlier legislation, the stipulations in this Bill are largely technical in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As long as we accept the premise that such excess reserve accumulation is reasonable, then their transfer to management by GIC is likely to be sound and potentially more efficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MAS protocol currently adopts a threshold where OFRs in excess of 65% of GDP are regarded as excessive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that this threshold is not established in law and is operationally determined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am not opposed to this, of course, but I am left wondering why such a specific limit would need to be hard-coded into the letter of the law since the functional use of RMGS purchases are, in any case, limited to reserve management purposes rather than fiscal expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One is also left to wonder how the 65% or, for that matter, the $580 billion threshold was determined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would these two amounts be consistent at all times?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, a 65% of GDP will continue to increase in absolute terms as the economy continues to grow whereas the dollar amount would not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would this mean a need for periodic revisions to the $580 billion?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would also add that since 2010, Singapore has been party to the Chiang Mai Initiative while the Federal Reserve has also extended temporary dollar financial swap facilities to Singapore since the Global Financial Crisis in 2008.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does the threshold already account for the additional extra liquidity available as a result of these swap arrangements?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Conversely, the abundant liquidity conditions currently in place resulting from large-scale asset purchases due to unconventional monetary policy operations such as quantitative easing appear globally to be steadily receding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Federal Reserve Bank has already announced tapering operations, many central banks have already begun the process of low interest rate normalisation and markets already anticipate tighter liquidity conditions to set in around the middle of this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the threshold be sufficient if we are no longer living in a world of abundant liquidity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The official reason furnished by MAS in its explanatory brief accompanying this Bill, is that appreciation pressure on the Singapore dollar is the result of "positive net saving and persistent capital inflows arising from abundant liquidity in global financial markets." But this only begs the question of why we appear to be resisting such appreciation pressure of which excess accumulation is but the consequence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The standard explanation is that MAS is mandated to pursue an exchange rate policy aimed at mitigating the effects of excessive short-term volatility in the real economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But minimising short-term volatility does not by any means preclude a steady appreciation – or depreciation, for their matter – over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially the case for countries that have experienced rapid economic growth as Singapore has since Independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, remarkably, our real effective exchange rate – that is, the average rate relative to our major trading partners – while waxing and waning over the decades has remained remarkably close to the level that prevailed in 1970.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we were still a middle-income country, this may have been a viable development strategy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, in as much as we remain an open economy reliant on competitive exports, we must not forget that there is also a flip side to such exchange rate undervaluation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not only does this drive up the cost of the intermediate goods our manufacturers use as inputs to production, it also indirectly impoverishes our consumers who must now face higher prices for the Nike shoes, Samsung TVs and Apple iPhones that we import from elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is all the more so in the current macroeconomic environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, this should be unsurprising given how much of our goods and services are in fact imported and as the Minister of State Low Yen Ling as well as Minister Indranee mentioned, global inflation is likely to remain elevated due to a mix of supply constraints, tight labour markets in certain segments and heightened fuel prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, both MAS and MTI have themselves acknowledged that this state of affairs is "likely to continue in the near term".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am not, of course, the first to suggest that our real exchange rate may in fact be undervalued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other observers using more rigorous assessment criteria have posited the same thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would, at the very least, urge additional introspection and research by MAS on whether there is in fact a potential undervaluation of the Singapore dollar, and to publish and share with the public the results of such research.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Speaker, our huge national reserves are the pride of our nation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But few Singaporeans know the size of our reserves and how the reserves are accumulated, managed and spent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reserves are actually accumulated through a mechanism which operates on a few key principles put in place in the 1980s by the late Dr Goh Keng Swee.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The mechanism essentially uses our large pool of domestic savings to soak up the foreign money that flows into Singapore because of its strategic position as a trade and financial centre of Southeast Asia since the late 19th century.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This mechanism has worked well and will put us in a strong financial position for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this MAS (Amendment) Bill that we are debating today will violate a key principle of this mechanism laid down by Dr Goh and runs the risk of compromising the mechanism altogether.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That principle stipulates that the Government must purchase foreign reserves from MAS with Government deposits, which is essentially the cash owned by the Government or the nation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, this is a major change in the conduct of a monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, let us bear that in mind, as I proceed through my speech today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My speech today will start off with explaining the reserve accumulation process and the dangers of the RMGS and then ends with a call on the Government to be more transparent about our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government, specifically MOF, oversees the reserve accumulation and management process, but it is the MAS and GIC which are the operating entities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MAS as central bank of Singapore has the power to print Singapore dollars as and when the need arises.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MAS is also the banker for the Government, holding the nation's cash in the form of Government deposits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MAS buys and sells foreign currencies with Singapore dollars on the Foreign Exchange Market to manage the value of Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When foreign currencies are bought, they become the Official Foreign Reserves (OFR) of MAS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under our reserve management arrangement, MAS will keep OFR up to a stipulated amount for managing the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The stipulated amount currently is about $325 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Foreign reserves in excess of the stipulated amount will be transferred to GIC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: GIC is a 100% Government-owned investment company formed in 1981 to manage the excess foreign reserves as an endowment fund for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlike the OFR, an endowment fund can invest in more long-term and risky investments to achieve a higher return.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As substantial assets have been transferred to GIC over the years, GIC holds most of our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The balance is held by Temasek Holdings, which is not involved in the reserve accumulation process explained here.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The OFR under MAS is also technically not considered part of our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given our position as a financial centre of Southeast Asia, there is usually a net inflow of foreign money year after year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the MAS has ample opportunity to accumulate foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The MAS can utilise the Government deposits or increase the supply of Singapore dollars to accumulate foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, the foreign reserves were mainly accumulated using Government deposits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have substantial Government deposits because it is actually our huge excess domestic savings, channelled into the public coffers through the CPF system and the structural Government surpluses derived from land sales and a whole range of indirect taxes and public services fee.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Accordingly, the accumulation of reserves is limited by the amount of excess savings we have.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what do we do when the inflow of foreign money far exceeds the amount of the Government deposits or our excess savings?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can decide not to accumulate any more reserves or to continue accumulating.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we choose the former, then we will have to either allow our Singapore dollar to appreciate further or to implement new policies to control the inflow of foreign money.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government wishes to continue accumulating foreign reserves, MAS will have to print new Singapore dollars since there is no Government deposits to pay for it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems to be the case in 2020 and 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When MAS probably increased the Singapore dollars to absorb the sudden surge in foreign money inflow.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This in turn has caused the accelerated rise in property prices from 2022 to today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the excess has to be transferred to GIC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, under the present rule the foreign reserves cannot be transferred from MAS to GIC if the foreign reserves were not paid for by Government deposits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government and MAS, a central bank, are independent operating entities, operationally.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the Government cannot take assets away from MAS without paying for it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill does open up the possibility for the Government to pressure MAS to print more Singapore dollars to accumulate foreign reserves and then buy them over from MAS with RMGS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Needless to say, this runs the danger of a collapse in monetary and fiscal discipline, leading to hyperinflation potentially.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, we recommend that there should be a strict annual RMGS, issuance limit, annual limit incorporated into the Bill, as a new check to reduce the potential dangers described above.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the first question I want to ask is we appreciate all the safeguards that the Minister for Finance had explained just now about preventing monetisation of Government spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, can the Minister explain what is the difference between the monetisation that you are explaining and the fact that in 2020 and 2021, we have accumulated assets, additional assets of close to $200 billion and at the same time, on the other hand, we have been spending for the COVID-19 packages.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, is this not indirectly monetisation of Government spending?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I shall touch on the transparency of our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has always been unwilling to state officially the size of our national reserves; often citing national security as a reason.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because the Government actually reports our country's financial position every year in a report entitled the Government Financial Statement (GFS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, a few of us – busy and pressured Singaporeans – know of this report.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because yearly, up to 2020, only one hard copy of the report was available at the National Library.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This report went online only after 2020 on SingStat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, we can assume that the intelligence agents of foreign countries would not have missed this piece of information.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, it is rational that the Government announces our national reserves, or at least the financial assets reported in the GFS in the mainstream media every year so that Singaporeans will get to know about it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, my second question is, does the Government still think that there is a need to keep our national reserves figures confidential?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our national reserves have continued to increase because we continue to accumulate new foreign reserves to the tune of about a $100 billion a year for 2020 and 2021, as explained just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of that, we also earned net investment return of about $40 billion for each of those years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By my estimate, the total financial assets will increase further to $1.5 trillion in Fiscal Year 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, it is puzzling, why the Government keeps insisting on raising more taxes when our foreign reserves are substantial, still increasing and earn good returns every year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, the Government should disclose the size of our national reserves to Singaporeans or at least confirm the information that is already made public.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should also account for the accumulation management and spending of the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, given our huge national reserves which are still growing and giving a good investment return, our country's financial position is healthy and there is no need to raise additional tax revenue through the GST.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans continue to ask me how about Government expenditures?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, many of them would like to know how the Government has spent the $100 billion for the COVID-19 packages.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will request the Government to submit a full report to Parliament during the Budget Debate on 18 February before it asks Singaporeans for more money through the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, there is an economic cost in accumulating reserves too, as what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also said just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is best to stick to Dr Goh's prudent style of reserve accumulation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Printing money to acquire foreign reserves, allowed under this Bill, will carry with it a big economic cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, if we really need this Bill, there should be at least an annual RMGS issuance limit incorporated into this Bill as a check on the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed $580 billion limit currently provided in the Bill is far too large and is not an annual limit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we request the Government to seriously take note of our concerns and not allow monetary and fiscal discipline to be weakened by this Bill.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The OFR that are transferred to the Government is for long-term management by the GIC.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, transfers of MAS OFR are mediated through a corresponding reduction in the Government's cash deposits held at MAS.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, with smaller fiscal balances in recent years, leading to a situation where the Government's cash deposits are not growing as rapidly as the MAS' accumulation of OFR, the current mechanism for transfer faces a constraint.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What has caused MAS to systematically accumulate OFR over these decades?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: How do we prevent the perception that the new mechanism offers the Government the means to conduct money finance fiscal policy?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When the Government does run a budget surplus over its term of office, which it has, the public saving augments the stock of reserves and boosts the country's net foreign assets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Net foreign assets denominated in foreign currency, such as the US dollar, has higher real purchasing power when measured in terms of domestic GDP because some of the goods and services consumed by Singaporeans are non-traded.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And in the classroom, we give the favourite example of haircuts.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Transport costs are too high to make it worthwhile to travel to another country to get a haircut, so haircuts become a non-tradable activity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Through this channel, an increase in net foreign assets tends to be associated in statistical analysis with a depreciation of the real effective exchange rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is the nominal effective exchange rate of the Singapore dollar, that is, how many Singapore dollars to buy a US dollar in the foreign exchange market; and then, there is the real effective exchange rate, which really measures Singapore's general price level relative to the general price level of its trading partners when measured in the same currency.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, when Singapore's cost of living goes up, we have a real exchange rate appreciation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Correspondingly, when things are cheaper in Singapore, because haircuts are not tradable, we have a real exchange rate depreciation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The channel I just refer to suggests that what you might call the valuation effect, tends to be negatively associated with our net foreign assets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Other channels, such as more rapid productivity growth in the manufacturing sector compared to the productivity growth in the non-traded goods sector, might exert pressures for a real exchange rate appreciation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, if you have the manufacturing sector able to robotise and so on, and its productivity goes up, whereas the non-traded sector, apart of the retail sector, which largely will be selling to only domestic customers and their productivity is not growing as much, then the fact that the manufacturing sector is experiencing higher productivity growth will push up the wage rate, but workers are free to move in the job between the factory and in the retail sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is an upward pressure in the retail sector, that is non-traded, also to pay as high a wage, whereas productivity has not gone up, so if unit labour costs goes up and therefore the non-traded good price tends to go up.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And for that reason, this channel leads to a real exchange rate appreciation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Another channel that can cause a real exchange rate appreciation is the rise of domestic investment, because a part of investment such as building infrastructure, tends to be non-tradable.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And that rise in domestic investment also tends to raise the real effective exchange rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, there are all these factors that can cause the real exchange rate to go up or to go down.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It somewhat declined down to the early 1990s and then began to rise again until the Asian Financial Crisis, came down again around to about 2005, and since then, has been rising.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, despite these forces that I have just mentioned that can cause real exchange rate appreciation or depreciation, with Singapore experiencing steady capital inflows, alluded to by Minister for Finance, including short-term capital inflows, has meant that the nominal effective exchange rate of the Singapore dollar has faced upward pressure to appreciate beyond the equilibrium real effective exchange rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, in the absence of the MAS intervention in the foreign exchange market, the Singapore dollar would tend to become overvalued.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, the RMGS cannot be used as a tool to print money to pay for Government spending.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Our being a small, open economy means that the management of the nominal exchange rate – I think that was very much in the thought of Dr Goh Keng Swee – serves well the purpose of achieving medium term price stability.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And we have the record to show for it, because other than the spike of inflation in 1973 and a smaller spike in 1979 during the oil crisis, we largely have maintained very stable inflation rate, below 2% per annum.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Structural policy, such as the implementation of Industry Transformation Maps, helps to raise the economy's underlying rate of productivity growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This in turn, contributes to growth of national income as a mature economy, because as a mature economy, it is not going to be capital deepening that will raise the standard of living.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A large part of what would contribute to our steady growth of income will have to come from productivity growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But with the growth of national income, we have an expansion of the tax base.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Fiscal policy in setting the tax subsidy structure contributes to economic inclusion.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, painting with a broad brush, we have three economic objectives: maintaining medium-term price stability, achieving an underlying economy wide productivity growth and facilitating economic inclusion with an assignment of three policy instruments: an exchange rate centred monetary policy, structural policy and fiscal policy respectively.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is a good step to take as it will also reduce MAS' exposure to translation effects from its foreign currency holdings.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The introduction of new safeguards along with the amendments to the Government Securities Act will help ensure that RMGS will be solely used for the purpose of transferring OFR.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The safeguards will provide assurance to the public that RMGS cannot be used for Government spending.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the above, I seek two clarifications from the Minister on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One can expect the exact percentage to be confidential and vary, depending on the conditions of the financial markets.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If more RMGS is issued, on average one can expect higher investment but lower liquidity cushion to manage the Singapore dollar exchange rate in times of financial market stress.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Conversely, if the size of RMGS is lower, the higher will be MAS' liquidity cushion.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As MAS being our central bank alone determines such levels independent of the Government, can Minister explain how this independence is maintained since MAS' board comprises largely of our Government Ministers who have roles and responsibilities on both sides?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Assuming a higher level of OFR is required to conduct monetary policy, it appears that MAS can redeem RMGS from the Government on demand.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can Minister explain how the mechanism ensures fairness between central bank, which may need more liquidity during periods when markets are under financial stress and the Government, or GIC, which has invested the RMGS funds in longer-term assets and may have to potentially sell assets under market stress conditions?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Putting aside the pandemic, Singapore could continue to have a high savings rate because of its tradition of prudent fiscal policy and the mandatory contributions all working Singaporeans make to their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given Singapore’s positive net savings and persistent capital inflows, the nominal exchange rate often tends to appreciate more than is required to keep inflation low and stable.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS accumulates foreign assets on average in the process of managing the Singapore dollar within its policy band even as it sells foreign assets during times of stress on the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Excess reserves should be managed by GIC as long-term investments and yield more returns.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, there is an opportunity cost when the transfer of reserves is delayed.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that MAS invests the OFR in a well diversified portfolio.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister share with the House how much of green bonds and green equities does it have in its portfolio?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MAS invest in more green instruments, especially those which are issued in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Reserves Management Government Securities (RMGS) be invested into green and sustainability-related instruments?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Were the official foreign reserves valued at cost or market price?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that MAS' accounting conventions adopted conformed to international accounting practice.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important that the people know the approach taken to value Government assets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Valuations should be derived from prudent principles and not based on optimistic assumptions to inflate asset values.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Has MAS' investment approach been to invest its reserves for returns?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will it be reducing its holdings in US dollars and GBP and diversified into other currencies?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS seeks to smoothen wide fluctuations in the exchange rate by intervening in the currency markets, selling Singapore dollars if the currency is deemed to have appreciated too much or buying Singapore dollars if the currency has been beaten down too much.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Reserves management is a multi-objective and a multi-generational effort.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The OFR serves as a buffer against bad times and as a Singapore dollar stabiliser.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS, like Members in this House, are custodians of our reserves and we owe a duty of care and responsibility to the current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MAS needs only a fraction of these reserves on hand to manage our domestic price stability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rest of it would be better utilised by our GIC, our sovereign wealth fund, to maximise investment returns.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill provides a framework for that transfer to happen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The framework delicately balances the need to maximise investment returns with the need to give MAS enough flexibility to maintain price stability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have four points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the definition of excess foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share details on the reviews MAS has conducted in order to arrive at this calculation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the 65% has not changed in the past three years, can the Minister share how regularly MAS plans to review the amount of foreign reserves it needs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, does MAS envision the scope for this 65% to be further reduced and for a greater proportion to be channelled for GIC investments?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is given the fact that even in the worst months of the Asian Financial Crisis and the Global Recession, we saw very minimal, if any, decrease in foreign reserves managed by MAS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, I understand future crises and currency speculation may demand unusually high amounts of foreign reserves to combat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This brings me to my second point on worst-case scenarios.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By design, GIC and Temasek's assets are less liquid and higher risk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, it seems unclear how the amount of foreign currency envisioned as necessary in such an extreme scenario could become quickly available.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about the redemptions of the RMGS by MAS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain what role will the Government play in setting conditions for the redemption of the RMGS by MAS?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam had said that MAS will have "sole discretion to redeem the RMGS for foreign assets before maturity and without penalty." Yet, section 15B(2) of the amended Act states that the Minister's agreement will be required in setting conditions surrounding a repayment and redemption of RMGS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This seems to contradict the notion that MAS will have sole discretion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It opens the door for a future Minister to institute a penalty for early redemptions or, indeed, any other kind of condition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share why the Bill does not provide MAS with sole discretion on redeeming the RMGS prematurely and without penalty?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What conditions does the Ministry expect to set in relation to the repayment and redemption of the RMGS?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth and final point is about the $580 billion limit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how it decided on $580 billion as the limit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the principle and methodology by which the Government has set the $580 billion as the cap?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In summary, I hope the Minister can clarify how MAS reached its definition of excess foreign reserves, how liquid GIC and Temasek's foreign reserves are, what role the Government will play in constraining MAS' RMGS redemptions and how the $580 billion limit was determined.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: RMGS will help to facilitate continued transfer of official foreign reserves, or OFR, to the Government for longer-term investment with GIC.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The goal is to help to promote financial stability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to seek the Minister's clarification on some issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that MAS reviews this amount regularly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As it is a key threshold in this arrangement for the RMGS bond issuance, do we expect this threshold to change over time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, what are the key variables that may shift this ratio?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that there will be a separate RMGS issuance limit, which allows for greater transparency on RMGS proceeds and clearer segregation from other Government securities and treasury bills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government will accept only foreign assets in exchange for RMGS issuance to draw a clear and direct link between RMGS issuance and transfer of OFR.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: MAS cannot sell its RMGS holdings to other entities unless the Minister for Finance consents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, RMGS cannot be used to raise funds from the market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry clarify how rigorously this policy will be enforced and under what circumstances might the Minister give consent?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, how can RMGS be liquidated to meet the transfer of foreign reserves back to MAS for intervention purposes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If MAS redeems RMGS bond before maturity at par to meet OFR requirements and support the conduct of monetary policy, how much loss can the Government provision for?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, since the transactions would be denominated in other currencies, would this make us more vulnerable to foreign exchange risks?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Taking the US currency, for example, will MAS be overly exposed to the US dollar holdings in its assets?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the inclusion of RMGS item in the MAS balance sheet with the passing of this Bill, can I seek the Minister to share what are the plausible worst-case scenarios from both an accounting, fiscal and market perspectives involved in undertaking these RMGS issues in the MAS balance sheet?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My last question concerns the impact on net Singapore dollar liquidity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the accumulation of RMGS on the MAS balance sheet over time have any indirect effect on the liquidity of the Singapore dollar in the medium to long run?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we continue with "leaning against the wind" activity as part of our band basket and crawl managed float, will this new RMGS introduction affect our overall sterilisation activities and net liquidity flows into the financial system in the medium to long term?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a good thing for financial analysts and the informed public who wish to have a more in-depth understanding of our financial situation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But can I clarify if there are plans to release higher frequency data going forward and, if so, will it reveal too much information to market participants and thus infer our foreign exchange intervention activities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The specifications in the Bill are clearly spelt out to segregate RMGS from other Government securities and treasury bills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: RMGS cannot be used to finance Government spending and neither can its proceeds be spent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it would not have any impact on our fiscal plans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nonetheless, the current transfer mechanism faces constraints as the accumulation of official foreign reserves persistently outpaces the growth of Government deposits in recent years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would be righted with the new RMGS mechanism.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, it is important to correct misperceptions that the policy is about financing the Government's spending and fiscal deficits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members' comments and queries can be categorised into a bucket of different issues and I will address them in turn.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Don Wee have all asked questions about how the optimal amount of OFR is determined and how MAS reviews this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS regularly reviews and updates the optimal amount of OFR for its needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In its reviews, MAS uses a range of internationally used reserves adequacy measures within a general cost-benefit framework to assess the required amount of OFR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: From a benefits perspective, the OFR provides MAS with the means to protect the functioning and stability of the economy against shocks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, MAS takes reference from historical episodes of such significant domestic and international disruptions to compute the OFR that is necessary to safeguard stability and confidence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: From the cost perspective, MAS recognises the opportunity cost of holding reserves in liquid financial instruments on its balance sheet in terms of the higher returns forgone, if these assets had not been invested in longer-term assets by GIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Singapore's economic and financial linkages with global markets continue to expand and deepen, the OFR required should broadly keep in line with GDP and complement the structural factors underpinning Singapore's macroeconomic and financial soundness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As we have repeatedly said, this is not a new idea.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The point about transferring excess OFR to GIC for long-term management is not new at all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is the very reason why GIC was set up in 1981.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, when Mr Leong Mun Wai talked about a departure from the principles that Dr Goh Keng Swee had set up – there is no departure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is completely in line and consistent with the founding principles upon which we do reserves management.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is also the question on the framework under which MAS manages the OFR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS manages the OFR with the primary objectives of maintaining confidence in Singapore's exchange rate-based monetary policy framework and securing macroeconomic and financial stability.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The key elements underpinning this OFR management framework are robust risk management, including an appropriate liquidity profile and a well-diversified asset allocation across geographies, asset classes and currencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These elements serve to produce a resilient portfolio and safeguard the OFR's availability to support MAS' conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Subject to these elements, MAS seeks to achieve good long-term returns on its OFR and that would include taking steps to manage longer-term risk like the impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In that regard, MAS would look at a range of instruments including green instruments which Mr Don Wee had mentioned.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both the risk management approach and asset allocation are approved by the MAS Board and reviewed regularly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Don Wee also asked if MAS values the OFR at cost or market price.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS publishes OFR data on a monthly basis and the published OFR is valued at cost.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This reflects our conservative accounting approach as a central bank.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The next set of questions pertains to risks that RMGS may pose to MAS' operations and balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked how MAS' autonomy can be ensured when subscribing for RMGS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS has always been operating independently within the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS' principal objective of maintaining price stability is stipulated in the MAS Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Under the law, MAS' Board of Directors is responsible for the policy and general administration of MAS' affairs and business, and in upholding the MAS Act, ensures that MAS conducts monetary policy to meet its price stability mandate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Furthermore, MAS can only subscribe for RMGS to facilitate the transfer of OFR beyond what it requires to conduct monetary policy and ensure financial stability.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS would also have the right to redeem RMGS before maturity at par, to meet its OFR needs and carry out its mandate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these safeguards are all set out very clearly in the Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: RMGS transactions are between entities within the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the whole-of-Government level, there is no change in our total foreign reserves and no additional exposure to foreign exchange risk.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For MAS, its subscription for RMGS will result in a change in assets from OFR denominated in foreign currency to RMGS denominated in Sing dollar.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This reduces the exchange rate risk for MAS by lowering its foreign exchange exposure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Correspondingly, the exposure to currency fluctuations, along with the returns on investments, are in turn borne by the Government, inherently as part of its larger portfolio of investment placed with GIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked if the accumulation of RMGS on MAS' balance sheet over time will affect the level of liquidity in the banking system and consequently, MAS' monetary operations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is because MAS uses only foreign assets to subscribe for RMGS and does not create or use Sing dollar in the process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is aligned with the frequency for the publication of OFR data, which is in line with international standards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Changes in the OFR are influenced by other factors besides intervention operations and transfers to the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These include changes in the stock of Foreign Exchange swaps as part of MAS’ money market operations to manage liquidity in the banking system, investment gains or losses on the OFR and currency translation effects on the OFR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In addition, data on Singapore's foreign exchange intervention operations is already separately disclosed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS publishes its net purchases of foreign exchange from intervention operations on a six-month aggregated basis, with a three-month lag from the end of the period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this addresses questions relating to risks to the MAS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The third set of questions is on the characteristics of RMGS, such as its maturity and early redemption features.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim queried about the basis and purpose of the $580 billion issuance limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, they thought that there might not be a need for such a limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the other hand, Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested to tighten and have an annual limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have set this limit so that the Government can administer and monitor the size of the RMGS issuance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having such a limit will provide transparency to Parliament, which serves as an additional layer of check.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, indeed, we could have done away with it completely but we thought that it would be prudent and will provide an additional layer of check for the Government to come back to Parliament to raise the limit should the need arise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Any such further increase to this limit will have to be justified by the Government and approved by Parliament and President.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked about the maturity period for RMGS issuances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The purpose of issuing RMGS is to facilitate the transfer of OFR for longer-term investment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi noted that there may be periods where the OFR falls below the optimal range and may need to be topped up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He asked how RMGS could be liquidated to meet MAS’ needs and whether there may be circumstances under which MAS might transfer its RMGS holdings to other entities, with the consent of the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The answer to this is that the optimal amount of OFR which is, as I said, sized at 65% to 75% of GDP, is not an insignificant amount and is expected to meet MAS' needs comfortably under most circumstances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To date, there has not been a crisis where MAS' OFR has fallen below this threshold.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, MAS’ OFR will only need to be topped up in a highly unlikely crisis of unprecedented scale, or what we call a "tail-risk event".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When MAS redeems the RMGS, the Government will transfer an equivalent amount of foreign assets to MAS, supplementing the OFR on MAS’ balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This upholds the intent of the RMGS by restricting MAS’ transfers of RMGS holdings to other entities to very exceptional and extreme situations, as determined by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To be clear, even if such a transfer were to take place, the effectiveness of the proposed legislative safeguards including those to prevent monetary financing, would not be diminished, irrespective of the entities owning the RMGS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think there was also a question whether a future government can introduce conditions that compromise MAS’ ability to redeem RMGS and why the Bill does not provide for MAS with the sole discretion on redeeming the RMGS prematurely and why allow the Government to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government will not be able to compromise MAS’ ability to redeem RMGS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I explained earlier, the terms for issuance of RMGS, including its conditions as to repayment and redemption, will need to be mutually agreed between MAS and the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Operationally, MAS and the Government will set the conditions to give MAS the right to redeem RMGS at par before maturity, meaning it can exercise this right at its discretion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government may choose to redeem RMGS before maturity if it has excess Singapore dollar liquidity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Allowing the Government to do so does not compromise MAS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS will not be worse off because the amount of OFR held remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Several Members asked how RMGS will affect GIC’s investment and liquidity management, including the implications if RMGS is redeemed before maturity at par to meet MAS’ OFR needs and how the foreign reserves managed by GIC could be made available to MAS in such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The introduction of RMGS facilitates the transfer of OFR not needed by MAS to the Government for longer-term investment by GIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I said, the mechanism may be new but the transfers of such OFR is not new.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: GIC manages the transferred OFR and other Government assets in accordance with its mandate given by the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As a long-term investor, GIC will look at long-term opportunities including sustainability opportunities and green investment opportunities, which several Members talked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The existing arrangement between MAS and the Government already ensures that foreign reserves held by the Government are available to support MAS’ operations if the need arises.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government has in place processes to withdraw assets from GIC for various needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Therefore, liquidity needs pertaining to RMGS are already catered for.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even in the unlikely case where the redemption exceeds what had been catered for, the Government can still repay MAS with assets which qualify as OFR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is no need for GIC to liquidate assets prematurely just to raise cash to repay MAS, in the event of early redemption.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, there was a question by Assoc Prof Lim on whether or not MAS deliberately keeps the exchange rate low for competitiveness reasons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS' aim is price stability over the medium term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are quite clear that keeping the Singapore dollar artificially weak is unsustainable and not in Singapore's interest.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The real exchange rate, not the nominal but the real exchange rate, is the outcome of price adjustments in Singapore's economy relative to that in other partner economies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So long as monetary policy here is set pre-emptively with the objective of medium-term price stability, then the real exchange rate will in time be in line and appropriate to economic fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we fully intend for that to be the case.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, besides some of the points which I had addressed, set out quite a number of points which I found quite puzzling.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is almost as though he had not read the full text of the Bill or listened to what I had said earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because I had set out very clearly in my opening speech that there are all these various safeguards and provisions which ensure that there is no room for monetary financing with this new RMGS mechanism.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is not a major departure at all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is simply a new mechanism to facilitate the transfer of excess OFR from MAS to the Government for long-term investments by GIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Such transfers have been happening since 1981 when GIC was formed and continue till today except with a new mechanism called "RMGS".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not intend to do any form of monetary financing and there are safeguards in the Bill to ensure this does not take place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the hypothetical scenarios that Mr Leong had set out in his speech about hyperinflation, monetary financing, these will not arise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is to be expected because GIC has a higher return-seeking portfolio than MAS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having said that, this increase is not expected to be significant, at least in the short term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Under the Net Investment Returns Framework, or NIR Framework, changes in the net asset base are smoothed over time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Any longer-term returns would also take time to materialise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our medium- to long-term fiscal projections have already built in this practice of continuous transfers to get back to the optimal range and have accounted for the higher expected return from OFR being invested by GIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That said, it is also possible that we will face a structurally lower rate of return on our investments over the long term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is due to the significant headwinds in the external environment, including elevated debt, moderation in growth, ageing populations and low productivity in many countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have explained this in this House on several occasions and it is consistent with reports by well managed long-term global funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Furthermore, investments come with risk and there will be volatility from time to time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no guarantee that NIRC will always be increasing every year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, on the spending side, on the expenditure side, we do expect expenditures to go up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A decade later, from 2016 to 2020, we are looking at 18% of GDP; 3% of GDP increase, which is about $15 billion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we do expect that to increase further in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will have to continue to rely on both NIRC and other revenue measures to meet our growing fiscal needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having diverse sources of revenues will also give us the confidence to plan ahead for the long-term growth of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I will elaborate on these issues in the coming Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is not the occasion to talk about fiscal projections.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I just wanted to give an explanation in response to the questions that were raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On transparency, a point that Mr Leong Mun Wai mentioned, in fact, a lot of information has already been put out in the public domain about how we manage reserves, about the different entities that look after our reserves – Temasek, GIC, MAS – their investment approaches.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We can never predict what these scenarios will be.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not just about an economic or financial crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It could be a pandemic, as we have experienced.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It could be actions taken by a hostile external actor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have two questions for the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is, yes, we may not need to announce another number for our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But would he agree that every year, when the Government financial statements are published, the mainstream media should report our country's statement of assets and liabilities?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Meaning, the $1.4 trillion of financial assets, for example, will be announced in the public.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question is, can I ask what is the average rate of reserve accumulations in the past and what is the expected reserve accumulation going forward?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And he said that in a few years' time we will be accumulating – I mean, that is what I hear from what he said – that will be a lot of reserves to accumulate, you know?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is why I have suggested that we should reduce the limit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is for the media to decide what they want to report.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it is for analysts to also dive deeper into the statistics and to see if they want to produce analytical pieces around them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But where the Government is concerned, we already put out a lot of information, as I mentioned, every year during the Budget, after the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will continue to review what additional information we might put out that will be useful.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
